statement: Data entry errors and incomplete legal documentation fall under the Basel level 1 category execution, delivery, and process management.
explanation: Processing errors and missing or incomplete documentation are standard examples of execution, delivery, and process management (EDPM).
originalText: Data entry errors and incomplete legal documentation fall under execution, delivery, and process management.

statement: Internal fraud and external fraud belong to the same Basel level 1 event risk category.
explanation: Internal fraud and external fraud are two separate level 1 categories; the split is by perpetrator, an employee versus an outsider.
originalText: Internal fraud and external fraud belong to the same event risk category.
correction: Internal fraud and external fraud belong to different Basel level 1 event risk categories.

statement: Losses from theft and hacking are examples of the Basel level 1 category damage to physical assets.
explanation: Theft and hacking by outsiders are external fraud. Damage to physical assets covers physical destruction such as natural disasters or destruction of equipment.
originalText: Losses from theft and hacking are examples of the damage to physical assets category.

statement: Vendor disputes are an example of the Basel level 1 event type execution, delivery, and process management.
explanation: Disputes with vendors and trade counterparties arise from failed process management, so they sit in execution, delivery, and process management (EDPM).
originalText: Vendor disputes

statement: Destruction of equipment is an example of the Basel level 1 event type execution, delivery, and process management.
explanation: Destruction of equipment is an example of damage to physical assets (DPA), not a process failure.
originalText: Destruction of equipment
correction: Destruction of equipment is an example of the Basel level 1 event type damage to physical assets.

statement: Employment contract termination is an example of the Basel level 1 event type execution, delivery, and process management.
explanation: Employment contract termination issues are an example of employment practices and workplace safety (EPWS).
originalText: Employment contract termination
correction: Employment contract termination is an example of the Basel level 1 event type employment practices and workplace safety.

statement: The Basel level 1 event type employment practices and workplace safety covers losses from acts inconsistent with employment, health or safety laws and from diversity and discrimination events.
explanation: Employment practices and workplace safety (EPWS) captures losses from breaches of employment law, workplace safety failures and discrimination.
originalText: Employment practices and workplace safety

statement: The Basel level 1 event type clients, products, and business practices covers losses from acts inconsistent with employment, health or safety laws and from diversity and discrimination events.
explanation: Those workforce-related losses belong to employment practices and workplace safety. Clients, products, and business practices covers client misinformation, product errors and regulatory fines.
originalText: Clients, products, and business practices
correction: The Basel level 1 event type employment practices and workplace safety covers losses from acts inconsistent with employment, health or safety laws and from diversity and discrimination events.

statement: Legal-risk losses are excluded from the Basel level 1 loss mapping because they cannot be cleanly mapped to any single level 1 category.
explanation: The Basel definition of operational risk includes legal risk, so legal losses are not excluded from the mapping.
originalText: She excluded legal‑risk losses because they cannot be cleanly mapped to any single level 1 category.

statement: External fraud is a high-frequency Basel level 1 category that is heterogeneous, containing both low-severity and high-severity events.
explanation: In industry (ORX) data external fraud is about 30% of loss frequency but only about 9% of severity: many small card frauds coexist with rare, severe hacking events.
originalText: External fraud is high‑frequency but heterogeneous, containing both low‑severity and high‑severity events.

statement: In industry loss data, the largest share of operational loss severity falls in the Basel level 1 category clients, products, and business practices.
explanation: Clients, products, and business practices accounts for about 52% of severity, driven by large regulatory fines and client compensation.
originalText: In terms of severity, the largest losses accrue to the clients, products, and business practices (CPBP) category.

statement: Damage to physical assets tends to produce among the least severe operational losses and has among the lowest frequencies of the Basel level 1 categories.
explanation: In industry data damage to physical assets accounts for only about 1% of both frequency and severity.
originalText: Damage to physical assets (DPA) tends to produce among the least severe losses and has among the lowest frequencies.

statement: Losses caused by defective software or IT system failures are assigned to the Basel level 1 event type business disruption and system failures.
explanation: Software and IT system failures, such as breakdowns and outages, are the core of business disruption and system failures (BDSF).
originalText: Business disruption and system failures

statement: Clients, products, and business practices is the Basel level 1 event category that most likely produces the greatest loss severity for a financial institution.
explanation: It accounts for over half of total loss severity in industry data because of large regulatory fines and client compensation.
originalText: Client, products, and business practices (CPBP).

statement: External fraud is the Basel level 1 event category that most likely produces the greatest loss severity for a financial institution.
explanation: External fraud is high frequency but only about 9% of severity. Clients, products, and business practices produces the greatest severity.
originalText: External fraud (EF).
correction: Clients, products, and business practices is the Basel level 1 event category that most likely produces the greatest loss severity for a financial institution.

statement: Execution, delivery, and process management is the Basel level 1 event category covering losses from failed transaction processing and from relations with trade counterparties and vendors.
explanation: EDPM covers failures to process transactions and manage processes, including vendor and counterparty disputes.
originalText: Execution, delivery, and process management

statement: Internal fraud is the Basel level 1 event category covering losses from failed transaction processing and from relations with trade counterparties and vendors.
explanation: Internal fraud involves intentional misconduct by employees. Failed processing and vendor or counterparty relations belong to execution, delivery, and process management.
originalText: Internal fraud
correction: Execution, delivery, and process management is the Basel level 1 event category covering losses from failed transaction processing and from relations with trade counterparties and vendors.

statement: A loss caused by back-office confusion that delays settlement of a trade with a counterparty is assigned to the Basel level 1 category execution, delivery, and process management.
explanation: Late settlement caused by a back-office process failure toward a trade counterparty is a classic example of execution, delivery, and process management.
originalText: Execution, Delivery, and Process Management

statement: Improper business or market practices is a Basel level 1 event risk category.
explanation: Improper business or market practices is a level 2 sub-category under the level 1 category clients, products, and business practices.
originalText: Improper Business or Market Practices
correction: Improper business or market practices is a Basel level 2 category under clients, products, and business practices.

changes.to: level 2 category under clients, products, and business practices

statement: A client lawsuit alleging that an advisor put commission and firm profit ahead of the client's best interest, a fiduciary breach, is assigned to the Basel level 1 category clients, products, and business practices.
explanation: Failure to meet a professional obligation to clients, such as a fiduciary or suitability duty, falls under clients, products, and business practices (CPBP).
originalText: Clients, Products, and Business Practices

statement: In the UK regulators' description of operational resilience, important business services mark the shift from a process-based view of continuity to a service-based view.
explanation: Important business services identify the services whose disruption would cause intolerable harm to consumers or market integrity, replacing the process-by-process view.
originalText: Important business services: From a process‑based view of continuity, the regulator moved to a service‑based view to ensure continuity

statement: In the UK regulators' description of operational resilience, the continuity of business services component requires firms to respond to disruptions, maintain trust among key stakeholders and communicate clearly during a crisis.
explanation: Responding to disruptions, maintaining stakeholder trust and communicating clearly describe the management of disruption component, not continuity of business services.
originalText: Continuity of business services: To contribute to the stability of the system, firms should respond to disruptions, maintain trust among key stakeholders, and provide clarity of communication during a crisis
correction: In the UK regulators' description of operational resilience, the management of disruption component requires firms to respond to disruptions, maintain trust among key stakeholders and communicate clearly during a crisis.

statement: In the UK regulators' description of operational resilience, the lessons learned component requires firms to learn from past events and to cover predictable shocks only.
explanation: Lessons learned requires firms to learn from internal and external events and to improve resilience to unanticipated extreme shocks, not only predictable ones.
originalText: Lessons learned: Firms should learn from past events and cover predictable shocks only
correction: In the UK regulators' description of operational resilience, the lessons learned component requires firms to learn from past events and to improve resilience to unanticipated extreme shocks.

changes.to: improve resilience to unanticipated extreme shocks

statement: The Federal Reserve's 2020 sound practices for operational resilience require firms to reduce their reliance on third parties.
explanation: The guidance asks firms to manage third-party risk to protect supply-chain resilience, not to cut their reliance on third parties.
originalText: Firms are required to reduce their reliance on third parties.
correction: The Federal Reserve's 2020 sound practices for operational resilience require firms to manage the risks of their reliance on third parties.

changes.from: reduce their reliance on third parties
changes.to: manage the risks of their reliance on third parties

statement: The Federal Reserve's 2020 sound practices expect firms to monitor and report on the coordination and maintenance of business continuity management and IT systems resilience.
explanation: Business continuity management and IT systems resilience are pillars of operational resilience, and their coordination and maintenance must be monitored and reported.
originalText: Firms should monitor and report on the coordination and maintenance of business continuity management (BCM) and IT systems resilience.

statement: A strong operational risk management framework is necessary in order to achieve operational resilience.
explanation: Operational resilience is treated as a key outcome of an effective operational risk management framework, which is its central component.
originalText: A strong ORM framework is necessary in order to achieve operational resilience.

statement: The UK regulators' operational resilience approach is built around important business services, with impact tolerances tied to critical services rather than to individual processes.
explanation: This is what distinguishes it from classic business continuity planning, which was process-based.
originalText: Resilience is built around important business services, with impact tolerances tied to critical services rather than to processes per se.

statement: Operational resilience concentrates solely on preventing disruptions, since severe disruptions are assumed to be avoidable with sufficient controls.
explanation: Regulators and firms accept that severe disruptions will occur, so the approach moved from pure prevention to preventing, detecting and correcting incidents.
originalText: Resilience concentrates solely on preventing disruptions, since severe disruptions are assumed to be avoidable with sufficient controls.

statement: Operational resilience learns only from a firm's own internal incidents, since events at other organizations are not comparable.
explanation: Lessons learned come from internal accidents and also from events made public at other organizations.
originalText: Resilience learns only from the firm’s own internal incidents, since events at other organizations are not comparable.

statement: In the 2020 U.S. Federal Reserve guidance, third-party risk management and scenario analysis are among the building blocks of operational resilience.
explanation: Third-party risk management supports supply-chain resilience and scenario analysis supports preparedness for tail events; both are supporting pillars of operational risk management.
originalText: Among the necessary building blocks of operational resilience, the firm should include third‑party risk management and scenario analysis

statement: Incident management in an operational resilience framework involves establishing procedures for preventing all possible disruptions before they occur.
explanation: Incident management is about response and recovery plans; firms accept that disruptions will occur and cannot all be prevented.
originalText: Incident management involves establishing procedures for preventing all possible disruptions before they occur.

statement: The best operational resilience framework is a significant one-time effort that requires no ongoing attention or maintenance once established.
explanation: Coordination and maintenance of resilience activities must be monitored and reported, and firms must keep learning and improving.
originalText: The best operational resilience framework is a significant one‑time effort that does not require ongoing attention or maintenance once it has been established

statement: The U.S. Federal Reserve issued its Sound Practices to Strengthen Operational Resilience in 2020.
explanation: The Federal Reserve is one of the key regulators with official operational resilience guidance, alongside the UK authorities and the Basel Committee.
originalText: U.S. Federal Reserve.

statement: The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision issued its seven Principles for Operational Resilience in March 2021.
explanation: The BCBS principles are one of the three main sets of official operational resilience guidance, alongside the UK and U.S. guidance.
originalText: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision.

statement: Among the BCBS principles for operational resilience, mapping interconnections and interdependencies and incident management directly address providing critical services with minimal or no disruption.
explanation: Knowing the dependencies needed to deliver critical services and having response and recovery plans mirror the UK approach to keeping critical services running.
originalText: Mapping interconnections and interdependencies; incident management.

statement: UK regulators expect firms to identify their important business services and develop an impact tolerance for each of them.
explanation: An impact tolerance quantifies the amount of disruption that can be tolerated for each important business service.
originalText: Develop an impact tolerance for each of the important business services provided by the firm.

statement: Under UK operational resilience expectations, lines of communication should be established immediately after a breach incident has occurred.
explanation: Communication must be planned in advance as part of management of disruption; setting it up only after an incident is too late.
originalText: Immediately establish lines of communication after a breach incident has occurred.
correction: Under UK operational resilience expectations, lines of communication should be established before a breach incident occurs.

changes.from: immediately after a breach incident has occurred

statement: An operational resilience framework should consider the continuity of important business services in both extreme and nonextreme situations.
explanation: Resilience is organised around important business services and must hold up in severe as well as ordinary disruptions.
originalText: continuity of important business services in extreme and nonextreme situations.

statement: An operational resilience framework should consider the continuity of important business services in nonextreme situations only.
explanation: Regulators expect extreme events to occur, infrequently, so the framework must cover extreme as well as nonextreme situations.
originalText: continuity of important business services in nonextreme situations only.
correction: An operational resilience framework should consider the continuity of important business services in both extreme and nonextreme situations.

changes.to: in both extreme and nonextreme situations

statement: An operational resilience framework should be built on the continuity of each business process rather than on important business services.
explanation: The old process-based view has been replaced by a service-based view centred on important business services.
originalText: continuity of each business process and recovery on a timely basis in extreme and nonextreme situations.

statement: A bank should aim to prevent all severe operational disruptions through strong preventive controls, treating planning for response and recovery as secondary.
explanation: Operational resilience assumes severe disruptions will occasionally occur, so frameworks balance preventing, detecting and correcting incidents rather than relying on prevention alone.
originalText: The bank should aim to prevent all severe operational disruptions, because regulators expect that with strong enough preventive controls such disruptions will not occur, so planning for response and recovery is secondary.

statement: Under operational resilience expectations, impact tolerance quantifies the amount of disruption that can be tolerated; it resembles a recovery time objective but is tied to critical services rather than individual processes.
explanation: Impact tolerance is similar to a recovery time objective, but it applies to important business services rather than to processes.
originalText: The bank should set impact tolerance levels by quantifying the amount of disruption that could be tolerated, which resembles a recovery time objective but is tied to critical services rather than individual processes.

statement: Under operational resilience expectations, a bank should learn from its own incidents and from events made public at other firms and continuously improve its ability to withstand unanticipated extreme shocks.
explanation: Lessons learned from internal and external events is what differentiates resilience from traditional business continuity.
originalText: The bank should learn from its own incidents and from events made public at other firms and continuously improve its ability to withstand unanticipated extreme shocks.

statement: Validating the operational risk management framework and ensuring it is reviewed periodically is a responsibility of the board of directors rather than of senior management.
explanation: The board approves the framework and ensures its periodic revision, and obtains assurance that senior management implements it effectively.
originalText: Validating the ORMF and ensuring it is reviewed periodically, so that the bank’s operational risks are properly identified and managed.

statement: Translating the operational risk management framework into specific policies and procedures that can be implemented and verified within each business unit is a responsibility of the board of directors rather than of senior management.
explanation: This is implementation work that belongs to senior management; the board oversees it.
originalText: Translating the ORMF into specific policies and procedures that can be implemented and verified within each business unit.
correction: Translating the operational risk management framework into specific policies and procedures that can be implemented and verified within each business unit is a responsibility of senior management rather than of the board of directors.

changes.from: the board of directors rather than of senior management
changes.to: senior management rather than of the board of directors

statement: Recruiting experienced technical staff and ensuring sufficient operational risk training to implement the operational risk management framework is a responsibility of the board of directors rather than of senior management.
explanation: Hiring and training staff to implement the framework is an executive task for senior management; the board only ensures adequate resources.
originalText: Recruiting experienced technical staff and ensuring a sufficient level of operational risk training to implement the ORMF.
correction: Recruiting experienced technical staff and ensuring sufficient operational risk training to implement the operational risk management framework is a responsibility of senior management rather than of the board of directors.

changes.from: the board of directors rather than of senior management
changes.to: senior management rather than of the board of directors

statement: The board of directors is ultimately responsible for operational risk management and resilience in a bank.
explanation: Responsibility can be delegated but accountability cannot; the board owns operational risk and resilience and oversees management's execution.
originalText: Board of directors.

statement: The chief risk officer is ultimately responsible for operational risk management and resilience in a bank.
explanation: The CRO is part of senior management and has delegated responsibility; ultimate responsibility rests with the board of directors.
originalText: Chief risk officer.
correction: The board of directors is ultimately responsible for operational risk management and resilience in a bank.

statement: The board risk committee makes recommendations to the full board on risk exposures and risk-based decisions and reviews larger operational risk incidents escalated from lower committees.
explanation: It sits at the top of the committee pyramid as a recommending and oversight body that advises the full board.
originalText: Making recommendations to the full board on risk exposures and risk‑based decisions, and reviewing larger operational risk incidents escalated from lower committees.

statement: The board risk committee sets the bank's risk appetite and approves the operational risk management framework without any reference to the full board.
explanation: The full board sets risk appetite and validates the framework; the board risk committee only makes recommendations to it.
originalText: Setting the bank’s risk appetite and approving the ORMF without any reference to the full board.

statement: The senior management team, rather than the board of directors, is ultimately responsible for operational risk management and resilience.
explanation: Senior management executes tasks delegated by the board and is accountable for them, but ultimate responsibility rests with the board of directors.
originalText: The senior management team.
correction: The board of directors, rather than the senior management team, is ultimately responsible for operational risk management and resilience.

changes.from: The senior management team, rather than the board of directors,
changes.to: The board of directors, rather than the senior management team,

statement: A risk management unit that reports through a risk-generating business line, such as the head of credit, lacks independence and should instead have a reporting structure independent of the risk-generating units.
explanation: The second line must be independent of the units that generate risk so that it can challenge them objectively.
originalText: The RMU lacks independence because it reports through a risk‑generating business line; it should have a reporting structure independent of the risk‑generating units.

statement: Placing a risk management unit inside a credit business unit improves its independence by bringing it closer to the risk it monitors.
explanation: Embedding risk management in a business unit removes its independence and creates a self-review threat; the second line should be independent of risk-generating units.
originalText: Independence would be improved by moving the RMU inside the credit unit so it sits closer to the risk it monitors.

statement: Independent external auditors provide independent assurance to stakeholders such as regulators and investors from outside the bank's three internal lines of defense.
explanation: External auditors sit outside the firm's internal lines, which is why they are sometimes informally called a fourth line.
originalText: The independent external auditors

statement: A bank's internal audit function is outside the three internal lines of defense.
explanation: Internal audit is the third of the three internal lines of defense; the first line is the business and the second line is the risk oversight function.
originalText: The bank’s internal audit function
correction: A bank's internal audit function is the third of its three internal lines of defense.

changes.from: is outside the three internal lines of defense
changes.to: is the third of its three internal lines of defense

statement: Internal audit independently assesses the control system and compliance with policies across all departments, including the risk function, and reports to a non-executive director.
explanation: As the third line, internal audit does not manage the risks it assesses and reports in solid line to a non-executive director such as the audit committee chair.
originalText: Internal audit team.

statement: Establishing risk management methods and measurement methods is a role of the second line of defense.
explanation: The second line owns the methodology, while the first line owns the risks.
originalText: Establishing risk management methods and measurement methods.

statement: Making decisions for managing risks is a role of the second line of defense rather than of the first line.
explanation: Risk-taking decisions belong to the first line; the second line challenges rather than decides.
originalText: Making decisions for managing risks.
correction: Making decisions for managing risks is a role of the first line of defense rather than of the second line.

changes.from: the second line of defense rather than of the first line
changes.to: the first line of defense rather than of the second line

statement: The second line of defense oversees the risk management activities of the third line of defense.
explanation: The second line does not oversee internal audit; internal audit independently reviews the second line.
originalText: Overseeing the risk management activities of the third line of defense.

statement: First-line risk owners monitor and report the operational risk profile of their business unit and escalate loss events and control deficiencies to the second line.
explanation: Risk owners manage and report the risks they generate and escalate residual issues to the corporate operational risk function.
originalText: Monitoring and reporting the operational risk profile of the business unit and escalating loss events and control deficiencies to the second line

statement: Developing and maintaining operational risk measurement policies, standards and guidelines is a role of the first line of defense.
explanation: Policy and standard setting is a responsibility of the second line, the corporate operational risk function.
originalText: Developing and maintaining operational risk measurement policies, standards and guidelines
correction: Developing and maintaining operational risk measurement policies, standards and guidelines is a role of the second line of defense.

statement: Challenging the consistency of business units' use of operational risk tools and providing evidence of that challenge is a role of the first line of defense.
explanation: Effective challenge of business unit practice is the role of the second line.
originalText: Challenging the consistency of the business units’ use of operational risk tools and providing evidence of that challenge
correction: Challenging the consistency of business units' use of operational risk tools and providing evidence of that challenge is a role of the second line of defense.

statement: In the three lines of defense model, the first line defines the organization's risk appetite but should not attempt to directly influence its risk culture.
explanation: Risk appetite is a board and senior management matter, and risk culture is shaped across the organization, including by the first line.
originalText: The first line defines the organization’s risk appetite but should not attempt to directly influence its risk culture

statement: In the three lines of defense model, the first line is responsible for implementing and maintaining effective controls to manage material operational risks.
explanation: Risk owners in the first line identify risks and establish and assess the controls over them.
originalText: The first line is responsible for implementing and maintaining effective controls to manage material operational risks

statement: In the three lines of defense model, the second line is part of management and owns the operational risk methodology, while supporting the first line to help the firm create and protect value.
explanation: The 2021 IIA model places the second line within management, providing expertise, support and challenge.
originalText: The second line is part of management (and owns the ORM methodology) but provides support to the first line in order to help the firm create and protect value

statement: Internal audit cannot design or implement the operational risk management framework without compromising the independence of its assurance role.
explanation: Internal audit's value is independent assurance over the first and second lines; designing the framework would mean reviewing its own work. Framework design belongs to the corporate operational risk function.
originalText: Internal audit cannot design or implement the ORMF without compromising the independence of its assurance role.

statement: Internal audit should report to the head of the corporate operational risk function in order to remain independent.
explanation: Internal audit must be independent of risk management and report in solid line to a non-executive director, such as the audit committee chair.
originalText: Internal audit should report to the head of the CORF in order to remain independent.

statement: Business line management is not a line of defense.
explanation: Business line management, as the risk owner, is the first line of defense.
originalText: Business line management is not a line of defense.
correction: Business line management is the first line of defense.

changes.from: is not a line of defense
changes.to: is the first line of defense

statement: The corporate operational risk function should not challenge the business lines' outputs because doing so creates a self-review threat.
explanation: Challenging the first line's inputs and outputs is exactly the second line's job; a self-review threat arises only if the second line takes part in first-line activities or supplies the answers.
originalText: The CORF should not challenge the business lines’ outputs because doing so creates a self‑review threat.

statement: To preserve its independence, the second line should give the first line the correct answers to its risk and control self-assessments before the first line completes them.
explanation: The first line owns its assessments and the second line challenges them afterwards; supplying answers in advance creates a self-review threat and destroys independence.
originalText: To preserve its independence, the second line should give the first line the correct answers to its risk and control self‑assessments before the first line completes them.

statement: Internal audit should not rely exclusively on the work of risk management, compliance or finance, but should examine an appropriate sample of the activities itself.
explanation: Internal audit may rely on others' work only after assessing its reliability, and must perform its own independent testing.
originalText: Internal audit should not rely exclusively on the work of risk management, compliance, or finance, but should examine an appropriate sample of the activities itself.

statement: What defines a line of defense is the role and responsibility a function performs, not the name of its department.
explanation: Because lines are defined by roles, hybrid functions arise, and their first-line and second-line duties should be documented and kept distinct.
originalText: What defines a line of defense is the role and responsibility performed by a function, not the name of its department.

statement: Under the three lines of defense model, business line managers as the first line have the authority to take on risk exposures within the bank's risk appetite limits.
explanation: Risk is owned by the business, but only within the limits set by the board's risk appetite.
originalText: Business line managers, as the first line of defense, should have the authority to take on risk exposures within the bank’s risk appetite limits.

statement: Under the three lines of defense model, the risk management function should approve every transaction that creates a new risk exposure for the bank.
explanation: That would pull the second line into first-line decision making; the second line challenges and may veto breaches of limits, it does not approve every transaction.
originalText: The risk management function should approve every transaction that creates a new risk exposure for the bank.

statement: Under the three lines of defense model, the third line should continuously monitor the implementation of the risk management framework.
explanation: Continuous monitoring is a second-line activity; internal audit remains independent and provides periodic assurance.
originalText: The third line of defense should continuously monitor the implementation of the ERM framework to ensure its effectiveness.

statement: Reviewing and taking part in the monitoring and reporting of the operational risk profile is a task of the second line of defense.
explanation: The corporate operational risk function reviews and contributes to monitoring and reporting of the operational risk profile as part of its oversight role.
originalText: Reviewing and taking part in the monitoring and reporting of the operational risk profile.

statement: Identifying risks and controls in accordance with the group definitions is a task of the second line of defense rather than of the first line.
explanation: Mapping risks and controls is carried out in the first line; the second line only challenges it.
originalText: Identifying risks and controls in accordance with the group definitions.
correction: Identifying risks and controls in accordance with the group definitions is a task of the first line of defense rather than of the second line.

changes.from: the second line of defense rather than of the first line
changes.to: the first line of defense rather than of the second line

statement: When the three lines of defense model is applied to model risk management, model developers and model owners, as risk owners, form the first line of defense.
explanation: The first line owns and manages the risk it generates; the second line independently challenges it.
originalText: Model developers and model owners, as risk owners, form the first line of defense

statement: When the three lines of defense model is applied to model risk management, the second line of defense owns the model risk it oversees.
explanation: The first line, not the second, owns the risk; the second line oversees and challenges it independently.
originalText: The second line of defense owns the model risk it oversees

statement: In model risk management, the second line of defense should help the first line build the models and co-sign their validation so as to ensure consistency.
explanation: Second-line involvement in building or co-signing models creates a self-review threat and destroys its independence.
originalText: The second line of defense helps the first line build the models and co‑signs their validation so that it can ensure consistency

statement: Internal audit, as the third line of defense, provides independent assurance over the first and second lines, performing its own sample testing and relying on others' work only after assessing its reliability.
explanation: Internal audit must not rely fully on the work of other functions; it performs its own independent analysis on a reasonable number of samples.
originalText: It should have provided independent, objective assurance over the work of both the first and second lines, performing its own sample testing and relying on others’ work only after assessing its reliability.

statement: Developing operational risk policies and training programs, and rewriting them where they are inadequate, is a role of internal audit as the third line of defense.
explanation: That is a second-line role of the corporate operational risk function; an audit function that developed them would lose its independence.
originalText: It should have developed the operational risk policies and training programs and rewritten them where they were found inadequate.

statement: Publicizing the reasons for employee dismissals, if applied with unnecessary blame, may suppress the escalation of issues and incidents because staff fear being blamed for reporting them.
explanation: Visible discipline helps only if it does not create fear of blame; blame discourages reporting and undermines risk culture.
originalText: It may suppress the escalation of issues and incidents because staff fear being blamed for reporting them.

statement: Risk appetite and tolerance statements should rely on scenario analysis performed retrospectively.
explanation: Good statements are forward-looking and subject to scenario analysis and stress testing.
originalText: Perform scenario analysis retrospectively
correction: Risk appetite and tolerance statements should be forward-looking and subject to scenario analysis and stress testing.

changes.from: rely on scenario analysis performed retrospectively
changes.to: be forward-looking and subject to scenario analysis and stress testing

statement: Risk appetite and tolerance statements should provide reasons for taking or avoiding certain operational risks.
explanation: The Basel principles expect the motivations for accepting, declining or limiting specific risks to be stated.
originalText: Provide reasons for taking or avoiding certain operational risks

statement: Risk appetite and tolerance statements should be easy to communicate and understand.
explanation: Statements must be straightforward to articulate and comprehend so that they can be applied across the organization.
originalText: Be easy to communicate and understand

statement: Cascading a firm-wide risk appetite down into controls, limits and monitoring metrics through risk owners, control owners and metrics owners is good practice.
explanation: Cascading appetite into limits, controls and metrics, each with a named owner, is the recommended governance structure.
originalText: It is effective, good practice to cascade down the firm‑wide risk appetite into controls, limits, and monitoring metrics via risk, control, and metrics owners

statement: Risk tolerance is a broader, more general concept than risk appetite, which is more specific.
explanation: Risk appetite is the broad, firm-wide expression of the risk a bank is willing to take; tolerance is the more specific threshold for a risk or metric.
originalText: Risk tolerance is a broader, more general concept than risk appetite which is more specific
correction: Risk appetite is a broader, more general concept than risk tolerance, which is more specific.

changes.from: Risk tolerance is a broader, more general concept than risk appetite, which
changes.to: Risk appetite is a broader, more general concept than risk tolerance, which

statement: An organization's risk appetite should be sufficiently stable that it does not respond to external events or changes in market conditions.
explanation: Risk appetite should be forward-looking and reviewed over time, so it should respond to changing conditions rather than stay frozen.
originalText: An organization’s risk appetite should be sufficiently stable that it does not respond to external events or changes in market conditions

statement: A board-approved operational risk appetite should be translated into exposure limits, key controls and monitoring metrics, with a risk owner, a controls owner and a metrics owner assigned.
explanation: An actionable appetite is cascaded into limits, controls and metrics, each with a named owner.
originalText: Translate the appetite into exposure limits, key controls and monitoring metrics for the feature, and assign a risk owner, a controls owner and a metrics owner.

statement: A business line head who manages, maintains and monitors a risk within the stated limits of appetite and tolerance, as part of the first line of defense, is the risk owner.
explanation: Risk owners are first-line managers accountable for the risk within appetite and tolerance limits.
originalText: Risk owner

statement: A controls owner is the first-line manager responsible for managing, maintaining and monitoring a risk within the stated limits of appetite and tolerance.
explanation: Controls owners are responsible for designing and implementing controls and for their effectiveness; the risk owner manages the risk against limits.
originalText: Controls owner
correction: A risk owner is the first-line manager responsible for managing, maintaining and monitoring a risk within the stated limits of appetite and tolerance.

statement: Expected losses are a component of a bank's risk appetite statement.
explanation: Appetite statements are expressed through exposure limits, key controls and tolerated incidents, not expected losses.
originalText: Expected losses.

statement: Exposure limits at business-unit level are a component of a bank's risk appetite statement.
explanation: Exposure limits are a core element of an appetite statement.
originalText: Exposure limits.

statement: Limits on the frequency and impact of tolerated incidents are a component of a bank's risk appetite statement.
explanation: Tolerated incidents, meaning acceptable frequency and impact, are a core element of an appetite statement.
originalText: Tolerated incidents.

statement: Market manipulation and insider trading on the firm's own account fall under the Basel level 1 category clients, products, and business practices.
explanation: They are level 3 examples of improper business or market practices, a level 2 category under clients, products, and business practices.
originalText: Clients, Products and Business Practices.

statement: Insider trading on the firm's own account is classified under the Basel level 1 category internal fraud.
explanation: Insider trading on the firm's own account is improper business or market practices under clients, products, and business practices; only insider trading not on the firm's account falls under internal fraud.
originalText: Internal Fraud.
correction: Insider trading on the firm's own account is classified under the Basel level 1 category clients, products, and business practices.

statement: Misuse of confidential customer information falls under the Basel level 2 category suitability, disclosure, and fiduciary.
explanation: It is a level 3 example whose level 2 parent is suitability, disclosure and fiduciary, under the level 1 category clients, products, and business practices.
originalText: The analyst should classify the misuse of confidential information under the Level 2 category of Suitability, Disclosure, and Fiduciary.

statement: Improper business or market practices is a Basel level 3 category.
explanation: Improper business or market practices is a level 2 category under clients, products, and business practices; level 3 holds specific activity examples.
originalText: The analyst should classify the failure to deliver sufficient collateral under the Level 3 category of Improper Business or Market Practices.
correction: Improper business or market practices is a Basel level 2 category.

statement: A forged signature by an employee and a cyber-attack by an external hacker are classified under the same Basel level 1 event type.
explanation: Forgery by an employee is internal fraud, whereas a hacker is a third party, so the attack is external fraud; they are different level 1 types.
originalText: The analyst should classify both the forged signature and the cyber‑attack under the same Level 1 event‑type category.

statement: Insider trading not on the firm's own account is a Basel level 3 example under the level 1 category internal fraud.
explanation: Level 3 lists specific activity examples, such as forgery, bribes and kickbacks, and insider trading not on the firm's account.
originalText: Insider trading.

statement: Theft and fraud is a Basel level 3 example under the level 1 category internal fraud.
explanation: Theft and fraud is a level 2 category of internal fraud; level 3 holds concrete activity examples.
originalText: Theft and fraud.
correction: Theft and fraud is a Basel level 2 category under the level 1 category internal fraud.

statement: Unauthorized activity is a Basel level 3 example under the level 1 category internal fraud.
explanation: Unauthorized activity is the other level 2 category of internal fraud, alongside theft and fraud.
originalText: Unauthorized activity.
correction: Unauthorized activity is a Basel level 2 category under the level 1 category internal fraud.

statement: In the loss distribution approach, losses within each unit of measure should be correlated and heterogeneous, while the many units of measure are aggregated under an i.i.d. assumption.
explanation: The approach assumes losses within a unit of measure are i.i.d. and uncorrelated, and dependence across units of measure is modelled, for example with copulas.
originalText: Within each unit of measure (UoM; aka, risk class), losses should be correlated and heterogeneous; however, the many UoMs should be aggregated according to an independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) assumption

statement: In the loss distribution approach, Monte Carlo simulation convolutes frequency and severity distributions into an aggregated loss distribution.
explanation: Simulated draws of frequency and severity are combined into the aggregate loss distribution.
originalText: Monte Carlo simulation convolutes frequency and severity distributions into an aggregated loss distribution

statement: In practice, loss distribution approach frequency distributions tend to be Poisson or negative binomial, while severity distributions tend to be lognormal, Weibull or Generalized Pareto.
explanation: These are the standard choices for modelling operational loss frequency and severity.
originalText: In practice, LDA frequency distributions tend to be either Poisson or negative binomial; severity distributions tend to be lognormal, Weibull, or Generalized Pareto Distribution (GPD)

statement: Because internal loss history is insufficient to describe the tail, the dataset likely needs to be completed with extreme value theory tail distributions and/or external data, where key decisions include scaling, cut-off mix and filtering.
explanation: Internal data are thin in the tail, so EVT and external data are added to the loss dataset.
originalText: Because the history of internal loss data is insufficient for the task of describing tails, the dataset likely needs to be completed with extreme value theory’s (EVT’s) tail distributions and/or external data must be added to the mix, where key methodological decisions include scaling, cut‑off mix, and filtering

statement: Combining a general loss modelling approach such as the loss distribution approach with techniques designed for extreme events, such as extreme value theory or scenario analysis, balances frequent smaller losses and rare catastrophic losses.
explanation: The loss distribution approach models the body well but copes poorly with very high skewness, so it needs tail techniques to supplement it.
originalText: A method that combines a general loss modeling approach with additional techniques specifically designed to improve the accuracy of extreme event estimation, effectively balancing both frequent, smaller losses and rare, catastrophic losses.

statement: Filtering is the method of combining internal and external loss data that sets specific criteria for including or excluding losses in the modelling dataset.
explanation: Explicit inclusion and exclusion rules also limit the potential for manipulation of results.
originalText: filtering.

statement: Scaling is the method of combining internal and external loss data that sets specific criteria for including or excluding losses in the modelling dataset.
explanation: Scaling adjusts external loss sizes to the bank's size (or for inflation); it is filtering that decides which losses are included.
originalText: scaling.
correction: Filtering is the method of combining internal and external loss data that sets specific criteria for including or excluding losses in the modelling dataset.

statement: The loss distribution approach fits separate frequency and severity distributions for each unit of measure and convolutes them into an aggregate annual loss distribution.
explanation: The 99.9th percentile of that aggregate distribution gives stand-alone capital for the unit.
originalText: Loss distribution approach

statement: Reverse stress testing fits separate frequency and severity distributions for each unit of measure and convolutes them into an aggregate loss distribution.
explanation: Reverse stress testing starts from a failure outcome and works back to the scenarios that could cause it; it does not fit loss distributions.
originalText: Reverse stress testing

statement: Extreme value theory is well suited to operational risk because operational losses typically arise from one main underlying cause that will generate larger future losses.
explanation: EVT requires a single main underlying cause, but operational losses have diverse causes, so this requirement is unrealistic and limits EVT's usefulness.
originalText: EVT is well suited to operational risk because losses typically arise from one main underlying cause that will generate larger future losses.

statement: Segmenting losses into homogeneous units of measure reduces the data available in each unit, making results less reliable.
explanation: The more homogeneous the units of measure, the less data each contains and the less reliable the fitted distributions.
originalText: Segmenting losses into homogeneous units of measure reduces the data available in each UoM, making results less reliable.

statement: The loss distribution approach cannot properly handle the very high skewness of operational losses without adding large losses, applying extreme value theory, or using scenario analysis.
explanation: Operational losses are highly skewed, so the approach needs tail supplements.
originalText: LDA cannot properly handle the very high skewness of operational losses without adding large losses, applying EVT, or using scenario analysis.

statement: The first step toward operational resilience is to identify important business services and map the dependencies between them.
explanation: Impact tolerances and severe but plausible scenario tests are then applied at the service level.
originalText: Identify important business services and map the dependencies between these services.

statement: Under operational resilience expectations, a firm should develop an impact tolerance for each of its internal processes.
explanation: Impact tolerances are set for important business services, not for every internal process; a process-level focus is the business continuity approach.
originalText: Develop an impact tolerance for each of the internal processes performed by the firm.
correction: Under operational resilience expectations, a firm should develop an impact tolerance for each of its important business services.

changes.to: each of its important business services

statement: An operational resilience framework should be non-complex and resource-light in generation.
explanation: Mapping dependencies and critical paths is complex and needs large teams, data and a multi-disciplinary approach, with operational risk management usually as coordinator.
originalText: The framework should be qualitative (because it complements the factor models), non‑complex (to achieve successful implementation), and resource‑light in generation (because participants already working on the ORM framework should not bias the resilience framework with dual assignments)

statement: Single points of failure are likely to be key risk indicators for operational resilience and, whenever possible, should be mitigated or removed.
explanation: They can be reduced through backups and redundancy.
originalText: Single points of failure (SPOF) are likely to be key risk indicators (KRI), and whenever possible, they should be mitigated or removed

statement: The important business services of an institution vary with the nature of the institution.
explanation: Not every process or service is equally important, so firms must prioritise those that matter for their own business and customers.
originalText: The important business services (IBS) vary by the nature of the institution, and prioritization assumes that not every process is important to an institution

statement: The key difference between resilience frameworks and business continuity management is that resilience is articulated around important business services.
explanation: Business continuity management is process-based, whereas resilience is organised around important business services with impact tolerances.
originalText: The key difference between resilience frameworks and business continuity management (BCM) is that resilience is articulated around important business services (IBS)

statement: After identifying important business services and setting impact tolerances, the next steps are to map the services and required resources, design severe but plausible scenarios, and review lessons learned and take action if tolerances are breached.
explanation: This is the order in the operational resilience process: mapping comes before scenario testing, and lessons learned follow a breach of tolerance.
originalText: Map the IBSs and required resources; design severe but plausible scenarios; if impact tolerances are breached, review lessons learned and take action

statement: A firm should design severe but plausible scenarios before it maps its important business services and required resources.
explanation: Scenarios to test delivery of a service cannot be designed before the service has been mapped end to end.
originalText: Design severe but plausible scenarios; map the IBSs and required resources; ensure communication plans are ready
correction: A firm should design severe but plausible scenarios after it maps its important business services and required resources.

statement: In most jurisdictions, developing a standalone cyber-security strategy is a mandatory requirement anchored in law.
explanation: Most regulators do not require regulated entities to develop a standalone cyber-security strategy; they expect a broader board-approved information security strategy.
originalText: In most jurisdictions the development of a cyber‑security strategy is a mandatory requirement anchored in law

statement: According to the Basel Committee report on cyber-resilience, all regulators expect regulated entities to have a board-approved information security strategy.
explanation: Although most do not require a cyber-security strategy as such, a board-approved information security strategy, policy and procedures is expected everywhere.
originalText: All regulators expect regulated entities to have a board‑approved information security strategy

statement: Many jurisdictions expect cyber-risk to be covered by the organisation-wide risk management and/or information security framework.
explanation: Cyber-risk is generally expected to sit within the broader risk management and information security frameworks.
originalText: Many jurisdictions expect cyber‑risk to be covered by the organisation‑wide risk management and/or information security framework

statement: Most supervisors review regulated entities' information security strategies, but very few require or evaluate standalone cyber-security strategies.
explanation: Supervisory review focuses mainly on the information security strategy rather than a separate cyber-security strategy.
originalText: Most supervisors review regulated entities’ information security strategies, but very few require or evaluate those entities’ standalone cyber‑security strategies

statement: Although regulators generally do not require a specific cyber strategy, they expect banks to maintain cyber-resilience capabilities under their broader oversight of technology, information systems and enterprise risk management.
explanation: Cyber-resilience is expected within the broader technology and enterprise risk oversight rather than through a mandated standalone cyber strategy.
originalText: Although regulators generally do not require a specific cyber strategy, they do expect banks to maintain cyber‑resilience capabilities under their broader oversight of technology, information systems (IS), and/or enterprise risk management (ERM)

statement: According to the Basel Committee, the chief information security officer should report to the chief risk officer.
explanation: The report sees a CISO reporting to the CRO as not ideal because of conflicting priorities; there is a trend toward reporting to the CEO or the board.
originalText: The chief information security officer (CISO) should report to the chief risk officer (CRO)

statement: Previously developed national and international standards cannot be leveraged for cyber-resilience because their scope is information technology or risk management.
explanation: Existing IT and operational risk standards can be and are leveraged for cyber-resilience.
originalText: Previously developed national and international standards cannot be leveraged for cyber‑resilience because their scope is information technology (IT) or risk management
correction: Previously developed national and international standards can be leveraged for cyber-resilience even though their scope is information technology or risk management.

changes.from: cannot be leveraged for cyber-resilience because their scope is
changes.to: can be leveraged for cyber-resilience even though their scope is

statement: Most regulators require institutions to implement the three lines of defense model for cyber-governance and prescribe precisely how responsibilities are distributed across the lines.
explanation: Regulators use the three lines model as an assessment lens but do not mandate it or prescribe how responsibilities are allocated.
originalText: Most regulators require institutions to implement 3LD and prescribe precisely how responsibilities are distributed across the lines

statement: The majority of regulators have adopted the three lines of defense model to assess cyber-security risk and controls.
explanation: Regulators use it as a lens for assessing cyber risk and controls.
originalText: The majority of regulators have adopted the 3LD model to assess cyber‑security risk and controls

statement: There is a greater supervisory focus on the first and second lines of defense than on the third line in cyber-governance.
explanation: Supervision of the third line receives less attention, which may hamper checks and balances.
originalText: There is a greater supervisory focus on the first and second lines than on the third line of defence

statement: Only a few jurisdictions have specific expectations on the independent reporting line from the chief audit executive to the audit committee.
explanation: Few jurisdictions address the independence of the audit executive's reporting line.
originalText: Only a few jurisdictions have specific expectations on the independent reporting line from the chief audit executive to the audit committee

statement: Regulator-set sector-specific cybersecurity requirements are most common in emerging economies with relatively homogeneous banking systems.
explanation: Homogeneity makes uniform regulator-imposed rules practical; the European approach is instead to examine whether firms have an appropriate IT strategy and security provisions.
originalText: emerging economy with a homogeneous banking system.

statement: When managers disagree over who should make the final evaluation of a cyber-risk assessment, the dispute should be escalated to the board and senior management, who are expected to oversee cyber-risk.
explanation: Ultimate accountability for cyber-risk decisions rests with the board and senior management, so neither functional manager can settle it alone.
originalText: escalate the report to the board and senior management, who are expected to oversee cyber‑risk and resolve the dispute
